subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the order and degree of the differential equation d²y/dx² = [1 + (dy/dx)²]^(5/3).

mark_split.label: Cube both sides to remove the fractional power

insider_note: Here the fractional power sits on the RIGHT side instead of on the highest derivative, but the clearing move is identical — cube both sides — and this time it leaves the highest derivative itself raised to a power greater than 1, so the degree is not 1.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Cube both sides to remove the fractional power
steps.margin_note: One mark. Cube both sides to clear the 5/3 power on the right-hand side.
steps.memory_tip: A power of 5/3 clears by cubing (raising to the power 3), which turns 5/3 into the whole number 5.
lines: This is now free from fractional powers.
steps.why: Cubing both sides multiplies the exponent 5/3 by 3, giving the whole number 5, so the equation becomes a genuine polynomial in the derivatives with no fractional power left anywhere.
common_mistakes: Squaring instead of cubing, which does not clear a denominator of 3 in the exponent.
Cubing only the right-hand side and leaving the left side as the plain d²y/dx².

steps.label: State the order and degree
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Cubing puts (d²y/dx²)³ on the left, so the highest-order derivative now carries exponent 3.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever cubing lands the highest derivative itself inside a cube, the degree is 3, not 1 — read the exponent on the LEFT side here, not the right.
lines: The highest order derivative present is d²y/dx², so the order is 2.
The exponent on (d²y/dx²)³ in the cleared equation is 3, so the degree is 3.
steps.why: Because cubing raised the highest-order derivative itself to the power 3, that 3 is the degree; the order still counts only how many times the equation was differentiated, which stays at 2.
common_mistakes: Reading the degree as 5 by copying the exponent that now sits on the right-hand bracket instead of on d²y/dx² itself.
Assuming degree is always 1 just because order-and-degree questions often come out that way.
